title: Charter Operators: "Don't Call Us Public"
author: Peter Greene
summary: Greene responds to a Wall Street Journal piece by charter operators Baker Mitchell and Robert Spencer, who complain that a Fourth Circuit ruling treating charters as state actors imperils the movement. The case began with a skirts-only dress code at a charter school run by Mitchell's company, but Greene argues the operators' real worry is that state-actor status would block the expansion of religious charters and other constitution-free arrangements. He points out that the charter industry itself spent years insisting these schools are public, even as operators claim private status when convenient. The piece is sharp school-policy commentary: if charters want public money and the public label, they must accept public-school rules, and the sector's ability to have it both ways may be ending.
points: The 'public' label for charters was created and defended by the charter industry, which undercuts the operators' complaint that a court merely followed convention.
Greene reads the operators' true objection as protecting the path for religious charters to take public funds without Establishment Clause limits.
The ACLU's point stands that ruling otherwise would let states build parallel privately operated public systems free of constitutional protections.
The argument reduces to being treated as private for rules and public for funding, which he says cannot hold indefinitely.
quotes: The case hinged on the question of whether or not charter schools are "state actors" aka actual public schools. The court said, "Yes, they are.

This is kind of hilarious, because the "convention" of calling these school public was created entirely, and purposefully, by the charter industry and its supporters. They have insisted loudly and often that charter schools are absolutely public schools, and have engaged in uncountable arguments with anyone who dares to say otherwise. Of course, they have also frequently insisted that they are private businesses when it's convenient for fending off state scrutiny or grabbing PPP pandemic relief money.

If charter schools are state actors, then that might get in the way of expanding religious charters. And sure enough-- we find amicus briefs filed by Catholic Charities of the Diocese of Arlington VA, Notre Dame Law School Religious Liberty Clinic, the Jewish Coalition for Religious Liberty, and the Religious Freedom Institute.

Well, no. They would undercut the extension of private religious organizations into a sweet, sweet chance to get their hands on public tax dollars while still enjoying unregulated freedom to indoctrinate some students into their religion while also discriminating against whatever students they choose to discriminate against in a taxpayer-funded Constitution-free zone.
Sure. Making girls wear skirts is one hell of a supercharged innovation. My usual offer stands--name one educational innovation that has come out of the modern charter school sector.

It's a tough call for the charter biz--if they aren't public schools, then at this point they really aren't much different from private voucher schools, so what's the point of them? But if they want to market themselves as public schools, they can damn well operate under public school rules.
